Home / World News / Zelenskyy says US-proposed Europe security framework could benefit Putin

Zelenskyy says US-proposed Europe security framework could benefit Putin "In my view, this can be dangerous," Zelenskyy told reporters on Friday. "This should not be the main agenda." His comments were embargoed until Saturday

Volodymyr Zelenskyy (File Photo: Reuters)

AP Kyiv 5 min read Last Updated : Nov 14 2026 | 7:40 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the United States had raised the possibility of a new security framework for Europe as part of efforts to end Russia's war in Ukraine, warning that Moscow could use such discussions to weaken Nato and reshape the continent's borders. "In my view, this can be dangerous," Zelenskyy told reporters on Friday. "This should not be the main agenda." His comments were embargoed until Saturday. Zelenskyy also said the United States had asked for the first time whether Ukraine would withdraw from parts of the Donbas region in eastern Ukraine that Russia does not control if Kyiv were admitted to Nato.

He said he believed Moscow was interested in reopening broader questions about European security rather than focusing exclusively on ending the 4 1/2-year war. "(Russian President Vladimir) Putin's desire to change borders in Europe is a fact. I am sure this is part of his concept of revising security guarantees in Europe," he said. "This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations."   European leaders have stressed that decisions about the continent's security must be made by Europeans themselves, warning against allowing Russia to dictate the terms of a new security order or negotiate Nato's future.

Also Read

Democrat Senators ask Musk to preserve documents on Starlink in Ukraine

US raised Donbas withdrawal in exchange for Ukraine's membership in Nato Zelenskyy reiterated that Kyiv would not surrender its territory. Ukraine is discussing a comprehensive security package with its partners that could include specific guarantees from Nato and the European Union, a strong Ukrainian military and financial support for a specified period, he said. It would also include a recovery plan, he said. "If the American side confirms precisely this to us, together with other Nato partners, then I will ask our Ukrainian society what it thinks: do we accept it or not?" Zelenskyy said. He stressed that any arrangement would not involve recognising occupied territories as Russian.

Zelenskyy also rejected the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality, saying that would require changing the country's constitution. "If Putin expects Ukraine's neutrality to be enshrined, that's not going to happen," he said. "We're not in Nato right now anyway." Zelenskyy says Europe must decide its own future Zelenskyy warned that broader discussions about Europe's security could allow Putin to seek changes to Nato's military presence, including the withdrawal of American troops. He said Putin had raised similar ideas with then-President Joe Biden in 2021, seeking a redistribution of power in Europe and the world. "I think Putin will bring up Finland and Sweden. I'm sure he will raise the issue of Hungary and the presence of American troops in the Baltic countries," Zelenskyy said.

He said any changes to Europe's security arrangements must be decided by European Nato members only after the war ends. "The sequence should be as follows: a ceasefire, an end to the war in Ukraine, and security guarantees for Ukraine," he said. "There can be no security guarantees in Europe, or for Europe, without Ukraine." Energy ceasefire and prisoner exchanges are priorities Zelenskyy said Ukraine's priorities in the Abu Dhabi negotiations included an energy ceasefire, reopening the Black Sea, prisoner releases and preparations for a meeting between leaders to end the war. He said Russian negotiators lacked authority to decide on several issues and that Moscow was unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire.

"At the meeting in Abu Dhabi, the Russian delegation said they didn't have a mandate to decide this issue, but we can also see that they are unwilling," he said, adding that negotiators had been told to resolve ceasefire questions directly with Putin. Zelenskyy said discussions in Moscow with US negotiators resulted in an agreement on a prisoner exchange involving more than 1,000 people on each side. The exact number was still being determined, he said, estimating it at 1,200 to 1,300. He also said Washington supported Ukraine's demand that European countries participate directly in future negotiations, rather than remain outside the main negotiating room.

Britain, France, Germany and Italy were among the countries represented at the Abu Dhabi meetings, Zelenskyy said. He expected between three and five European representatives to participate in future discussions. Zelenskyy questions Starshield restrictions Zelenskyy accused SpaceX of imposing restrictions on its Starshield satellite system in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory, saying the limitations were hampering efforts to intercept Russian drones. He said the system's speed had been restricted to a maximum of 161 kph (100 mph) in occupied areas and that the limitations had been in place for five days. Zelenskyy questioned the explanation that the problem was technical, saying the restrictions appeared to have been imposed by SpaceX despite previous assurances from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that Starshield was more under the control of the US government.

"The current Starshield restrictions suggest that SpaceX imposed them," Zelenskyy said. "That's what our team is telling me. So this doesn't quite line up with what we heard earlier. That's why we need to get to the bottom of all this."   He said the restrictions prevented Ukrainian forces from intercepting Russian jet-powered Shahed drones over occupied territory as they approached from the east, forcing them to wait until the drones reached areas where the limitations did not apply.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

item.title: US must respect India's right to self-defence, oppose terrorism: Blinken
item.description: "India is a global force," Blinken said, adding that the relationship and shared interests between Washington and New Delhi were "really global in nature".
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / US must respect India's right to self-defence, oppose terrorism: Blinken

US must respect India's right to self-defence, oppose terrorism: Blinken "India is a global force," Blinken said, adding that the relationship and shared interests between Washington and New Delhi were "really global in nature"

Former US Secretary of State Antony Blinken (File Photo: Reuters)

Press Trust of India New Delhi 5 min read Last Updated : Nov 14 2026 | 9:00 PM IST

Listen to This Article

The US must respect India's right to defend itself and should maintain a zero-tolerance policy towards terrorism, former US Secretary of State Antony Blinken said on Saturday, while describing Washington's ties with New Delhi and Islamabad as "fundamentally different". "India is a global force," Blinken said, adding that the relationship and shared interests between Washington and New Delhi were "really global in nature". In contrast, the US relationship with Pakistan is "regional," he said during a conversation with Jawed Ashraf, chairman of the India Trade Promotion Organisation, at the Hindustan Times Leadership Summit 2026 in New Delhi. "The relations with Pakistan are regional, and there are still going to be important areas where we need to do things with them, particularly, for example, when it comes to counter-terrorism, but these are fundamentally different relationships," he said.

"We have to have a zero-tolerance policy for terrorism. Period. And that means that we have to have respect for India's right to defend itself," he added. Also Read

Zelenskyy says US-proposed Europe security framework could benefit Putin

US wholesale inflation hits highest annual rate since 2022, PPI rises 6.5%

Trump says ex Apple CEO Cook is 'a legend', should replace Huang at Nvidia

Alembic bets on 30 US drug launches to sustain growth as exclusivity ends premium

Hegseth calls impeachment bid politically motivated, vows to fight removal

Blinken said the US approach must include support for India's efforts to respond to attacks as well as diplomatic efforts to prevent an escalation between New Delhi and Islamabad, the two nuclear-armed neighbours. He added that efforts to prevent escalation were important given the destructive potential of the weapons both countries possess. Reflecting on Washington's past engagement with Islamabad, Blinken said US strategic interests during the Cold War and the war in Afghanistan may have led successive administrations to be less critical of Pakistan's civil-military establishment.

"And there's certainly an opportunity for the United States to do more," he added. On India-US relations, Blinken described the transformation in ties over the past few decades as a shift from estrangement to a strategic partnership, underpinned by shared interests and people-to-people connections. "We moved from estrangement to a genuine and, in some ways, unique partnership, built on a convergence of strategic interests. Of course, it is also underpinned by the profound people-to-people connections between our societies," he said. He identified cooperation in emerging technologies as an important area for the two countries, pointing to collaboration in space, quantum technology and artificial intelligence.

"The next step is tech cooperation, our ability to work in space, tech, quantum, and artificial intelligence," he said. On India's relations with Russia, Blinken acknowledged the partnership's historical depth and said Washington did not expect New Delhi to sever those ties. "There will be places where we don't have the same perspectives. For Russia, we understand there is deep history between India and Russia. So, we don't want them to end it," he said. Blinken, who served as the 71st Secretary of State from 2021 to 2025 under then-President Joe Biden, said the world was at a profound inflection point, citing rapid technological change, inequality and shifting power.

"The speed and profundity of change is beyond anything we've seen, certainly in my lifetime," he said, noting that ChatGPT, an Artificial Intelligence (AI) chatbot, took one month to reach 50 million users, compared with 75 years for the telephone. He said the private sector increasingly drove technological change, while governments struggled to keep pace. Growing inequalities had fuelled a sense among younger people that they were being "left out, left behind", he said. Blinken warned that the US risked weakening its strength by damaging cooperation between the government, universities and research institutions, and by becoming less welcoming to skilled people from abroad.

"The biggest danger I think we face is a huge self-inflicted wound," he said. On US domestic politics, Blinken said the recent midterm results went beyond the usual setback for the party of a sitting president. He attributed the outcome partly to frustration over the cost of living and concerns about corruption. In the November 3 midterm elections, the Democratic Party won majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, shifting control of the US Congress away from Republicans. Blinken described the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran, launched in February by President Donald Trump, as "a war of choice" and said the first Trump administration's withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear agreement with Tehran had contributed to the crisis.

He said the agreement, signed in 2015 and formally known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), required Iran to ship out 97 per cent of its enriched uranium and placed limits on its centrifuges, while allowing extensive inspections. After the US withdrawal from JCPOA in 2018, Iran accelerated its nuclear programme, Blinken added, saying the ongoing military action would not resolve the issue. "It is very hard to try to force this Iranian regime to capitulate; it is possible to get it to negotiate. And these are very different things," he said. He called for an "off-ramp" to the conflict, warning that escalation could involve attacks on regional infrastructure, US bases and partner countries.

The Strait of Hormuz, he said, had become a major challenge for global energy supplies after not being a problem before the war. Since February, Iran has repeatedly restricted access to the narrow chokepoint, one of the world's busiest oil shipping channels. On the wider West Asia conflict, Blinken said a lasting settlement required resolving the Palestinian question and establishing a sovereign Palestinian state alongside a secure Israel. "There are seven million Jews in Israel. There are seven million Arabs and Palestinians between Israel proper, the West Bank and Gaza. No one is going anywhere despite what extremists on both sides would like to see happen," he said.

"The solution remains, I fully believe, even though this is not a popular view, a secure Israel and a sovereign state of Palestine," he added.

item.title: Listing may change 'Tata way', put profits ahead of philanthropy: Noel
item.description: Noel said while 'some people' are proposing a listing for group's holding company, he fears that enlarging the number of shareholders after a listing will shift its focus to profits from philanthropy ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Companies / News / Listing may change 'Tata way', put profits ahead of philanthropy: Noel

Listing may change 'Tata way', put profits ahead of philanthropy: Noel Noel said while 'some people' are proposing a listing for group's holding company, he fears that enlarging the number of shareholders after a listing will shift its focus to profits from philanthropy

The comments come at a time when ruptures at the top echelons of the country's largest conglomerate are out in the open | Image: Bloomberg

Press Trust of India New Delhi 6 min read Last Updated : Nov 14 2026 | 3:41 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Tata Trusts Chairman Noel Tata on Saturday expressed concern that a proposed public listing of Tata Sons could fundamentally alter the group's traditional business philosophy, warning that a wider shareholder base may eventually place profits ahead of philanthropy.   "My worry is that listing, which is what some people are proposing, will change the Tata way. And one day, if we have 30,000-40,000 shareholders, profit may take precedence over philanthropy. And I think that will fundamentally change the Tata way of working," Noel Tata said at the HT Leadership Summit 2026.   He said Tata Trusts would work with regulators and other stakeholders to find a solution that preserves the group's founding ethos.

"Tata Trusts will play a constructive role with regulators and others to try and find a solution which keeps the Tata way the way it is," he said.   The remarks come against the backdrop of an intensifying tussle between Tata Trusts and the Tata Sons board over the holding company's ownership structure and leadership. Also Read

Sunil D'Souza's elevation as Voltas chairman comes under the lens premium

Tata Sons listing: 'Regulator's verdict not a failure of advocacy' premium

Tata Sons rejects Noel Tata's request for Sept 17 board meeting recording

Tata Sons row: Philanthropy, rule of law not at odds, Parsi priest tells PM premium

Who is Sunil D'Souza, the new Voltas Chairman succeeding Noel Tata?

Tata Trusts, which controls about 66 per cent of Tata Sons - the holding company of the $165 billion Tata Group - has opposed a public listing, while the Shapoorji Pallonji Group, its second-largest shareholder with an 18.37 per cent stake, has backed a stock market float to unlock value from its investment.

The dispute gained momentum after the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) rejected Tata Sons' September 2026 application to surrender its registration as a core investment company, effectively closing a route the group had pursued to avoid mandatory listing as an upper-layer non-banking financial company.   At a September 17 board meeting, Tata Sons decided to initiate steps towards listing in line with RBI regulations and approved a fresh five-year term for Chairman N Chandrasekaran, reversing his August decision not to seek reappointment after February 2027.   Noel Tata opposed both decisions, with the Trusts subsequently questioning the legality of Chandrasekaran's reappointment. The board approved his reappointment by a 4:1 vote.

Emphasising continuity in the group's philosophy, Noel on Saturday said its ownership structure and institutional character had helped preserve its values across generations.   "The owner cannot die, the owner cannot be bought and the owner cannot retire. There is continuity in what happens the Tata way," he said.   The group has historically combined commercial operations with philanthropy and nation-building, with Tata Trusts playing a central role in its institutional framework.   On the group's strategic direction, Noel said there was no question about its broad objectives, but greater discipline was needed in executing large projects and allocating capital.   "Philanthropy on one hand. Nation building on the other. This is independence of leadership and personalities and this will continue. I do not question the direction of what we have done. I question, sometimes, the delivery of what we are doing," he said.

"The question is, do we have the discipline when we execute projects, and not the direction? How will projects with a long gestation period succeed if we don't have discipline? And how will we allocate capital to those projects?" he said.   "So, very clearly, the direction is fine, but we also need discipline in the execution of these very large projects," he added.   Highlighting the group's role in India's industrial development, Noel said Tata companies were participating in emerging sectors such as semiconductors and electric vehicle batteries.   "We are partners in India's development," he said, adding that the group was undertaking its first semiconductor project and setting up its first EV battery plant.

Noel also spoke about the growth of Tata's retail business, particularly Trent, which operates the Westside and Zudio brands.   He said Zudio was launched in 2016 to cater to consumers at the bottom of the economic pyramid by offering aspirational products at affordable prices.   "It was not that this aspiration for better product was only in the top metros or with the wealthy. The aspiration went down all the way. So we said, how can we address in a way the bottom of the pyramid? So in 2016, we launched Zudio to address this bottom of the pyramid with an aspirational product," he said.

The format started with air-conditioned stores of around 6,000 square feet, with prices beginning at ₹199, he said, adding that the starting price point had remained unchanged over the past decade.   On Westside, Noel said the decision to adopt a private-label model gave the company control over the entire value chain, from fabric and product design to retailing.   He said Westside, which began with doubts over whether such a retail format could succeed in India, now operated around 320 stores and was looking at expanding to more than 500.   Attributing the growth partly to rising consumption, he said demand had increased across socio-economic categories and markets over the past decade.

Noel also said the opportunity to address the needs of underserved sections of society had made a deep impression on him after taking over as chairman of Tata Trusts, adding that the experience had given him greater humility about the scale of social challenges in India.   Tata Trusts vice-chairman Venu Srinivasan and other trustees backing a stock market listing of Tata Sons are understood to favour greater transparency, stronger corporate governance and a clearer ownership structure for India's largest business conglomerate.   They argue that listing would subject the holding company to greater public and regulatory scrutiny, institutionalise decision-making and reduce uncertainty over succession and governance in a group whose businesses span multiple sectors. A public listing could also provide a market-determined valuation of Tata Sons and give investors greater visibility into the financial and strategic decisions of the group.

In a November 11 letter to fellow trustee Darius Khambata, Srinivasan and fellow vice-chairman Vijay Singh cited examples such as Novo Nordisk, Hershey, Lundbeck and Demant to argue that companies can remain anchored by charitable foundations while being publicly traded.   They also pointed to listed Tata companies, including TCS, Tata Steel, Tata Power and Tata Motors, which have undertaken long-gestation investments and nation-building projects without compromising their institutional character.   The Trusts would continue to retain their shareholding in Tata Sons and receive dividends to fund philanthropic activities, they argued, adding that greater disclosure would bring discipline rather than constrain the group's long-term ambitions.

item.title: Nvidia crisis: Senate panel summons Jensen Huang, Howard Lutnick to testify
item.description: Senior US officials are discussing Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's possible exit as lawmakers question the administration's oversight of advanced AI chip exports to China ...
item.dc:creator: Agencies
item.content:encoded: Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick have been summoned to testify next month before a Senate committee as Huang’s affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy raises national security concerns. Senator Tim Scott, Republican of South Carolina, on Thursday evening sent letters to Huang and Lutnick requesting their testimony in front of the Senate Banking Committee. “Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive United States (US) technology,” Scott said in a social media post, adding, “The American people deserve answers.”  Congressional leaders of both political parties have said they support efforts to hear from Huang directly about his entanglement with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who US officials concluded had been recruited by China’s main spy agency. Scott asked Huang to appear on December 3 by his own volition but also threatened that the committee could issue a subpoena. House Republicans also said on Thursday they were in discussions with Huang to testify before other committees. Huang has hired lawyers who previously represented executives in government investigations, according to people familiar with the matter. Senior White House officials are discussing whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick should be pushed out amid a spy scandal surrounding Nvidia’s now-former CEO Jensen Huang, two people familiar with the situation said on Thursday. A growing number of lawmakers criticised Lutnick for the administration’s refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a key US trade blacklist, and over whether the government was properly overseeing Nvidia’s exports to China. Criticism of Lutnick’s actions predates Thursday’s resignation of Huang, who said he would step down as chief executive officer (CEO) of the leading artificial intelligence (AI) chipmaker after reports of an affair with Alice Huang, whom US authorities suspect of spying for Beijing. But the charge that Lutnick has not done enough to restrict AI chip shipments to China has emerged as the fallout from Jensen Huang’s actions grows. Earlier on Thursday, a White House official said President Donald Trump “maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position.” In June, Reuters reported the Trump administration had held off adding China’s AI startup DeepSeek, memory chipmaker CXMT and over 100 other firms flagged as national security risks to a trade blacklist. Asked on CNN if Lutnick should lose his job, Republican Senator John Kennedy said: “I don’t know yet.” He and others have urged Lutnick to quickly publicly answer questions and noted he will be called to appear before Congress. “This is as serious as an aneurism.” The US has not posted any additions to that list since October 2025, the longest stretch between new postings in over a decade. Reuters earlier reported that the US Commerce Department has not added new Chinese companies to that list for fear of escalating tensions between the US and China. Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, who will chair the Senate Banking Committee starting in January, and incoming Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chair Chris Coons, a Delaware Democrat, wrote to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, telling the administration to preserve all documents related to Nvidia’s exports of advanced AI chips to China. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Friday his department had favored putting Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed on the US entity list for months but it was up to the Commerce Department to act, adding that the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) could possibly take other action. He added that the administration was working to shut down “leakage” in the chip export system.
